## Overview

Repeated measures over time often violate the independence assumption: adjacent
time points are more correlated than distant ones. Temporal correlation
structures model this pattern explicitly, improving both inference and
prediction.

This tutorial demonstrates four temporal correlation structures using
`nlme::BodyWeight`, which records rat body weights across 3 diets, 16 rats,
and 11 time points.

**Models covered:**

| Model | Structure | Correlation pattern |
|-------|-----------|---------------------|
| m_14a | AR(1) | Exponentially decaying: $\rho^{|t_i - t_j|}$ |
| m_14b | Toeplitz | Separate correlation for each lag |
| m_14c | MA(1) | Only adjacent times correlated |
| m_14d | ARMA(1,1) | Combined autoregressive + moving average |

**Packages required:**

```{r packages}
library(bayesreml)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(nlme)
library(bayesplot)
library(patchwork)
```

---

## 1. Data preparation

### BodyWeight data

```{r data-load}
data(BodyWeight, package = "nlme")
bw <- as.data.frame(BodyWeight)
bw$Rat  <- factor(bw$Rat)
bw$Diet <- factor(bw$Diet)
bw$Time <- as.numeric(bw$Time)

# Create a time index (1, 2, ..., 11) for correlation structures
bw <- bw %>%
  group_by(Rat) %>%
  mutate(time_idx = as.integer(factor(Time))) %>%
  ungroup()

str(bw)
cat("Rats:", nlevels(bw$Rat), "\n")
cat("Time points:", length(unique(bw$Time)), "\n")
cat("Diets:", nlevels(bw$Diet), "\n")
```

### Exploratory plots

```{r eda-spaghetti, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(bw, aes(x = Time, y = weight, group = Rat, colour = Diet)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ Diet, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(title = "Rat body weight over time by diet",
       x = "Time (days)", y = "Body weight (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Raw residual ACF

The autocorrelation function (ACF) of residuals from a naive model reveals
temporal correlation:

```{r acf-raw, fig.height = 4}
# Fit a naive model ignoring temporal correlation
naive_fit <- lm(weight ~ Diet * Time, data = bw)
bw$resid_naive <- residuals(naive_fit)

# Per-rat ACF
acf_data <- bw %>%
  group_by(Rat) %>%
  summarise(
    acf_vals = list(acf(resid_naive, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 10)$acf[-1]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(acf_vals = lapply(acf_vals, function(x)
    data.frame(lag = seq_along(x), acf = as.numeric(x)))) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(acf_vals)

acf_mean <- acf_data %>%
  group_by(lag) %>%
  summarise(mean_acf = mean(acf), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(acf_data, aes(x = lag, y = acf, group = Rat)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = acf_mean, aes(x = lag, y = mean_acf, group = 1),
            colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "ACF of naive residuals (per rat, red = mean)",
       x = "Lag", y = "Autocorrelation") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Strong positive autocorrelation at lag 1 that decays over subsequent lags is
the hallmark of AR(1)-type temporal correlation.

---

## 2. Constructing temporal correlation matrices

Temporal correlation matrices are constructed from the time structure and
passed to `bayesreml` via `known_matrices`. Each matrix encodes a different
assumption about how correlation decays with temporal distance.

### AR(1) correlation matrix

The AR(1) correlation matrix has entries:

$$
R_{ij} = \rho^{|t_i - t_j|}
$$

where $\rho \in (-1, 1)$ is the autocorrelation parameter. Since $\rho$ is
unknown, we fix a plausible value (estimated from the ACF) and let `bayesreml`
estimate the variance scaling.

```{r ar1-matrix}
make_ar1 <- function(n_time, rho) {
  R <- matrix(0, n_time, n_time)
  for (i in seq_len(n_time)) {
    for (j in seq_len(n_time)) {
      R[i, j] <- rho^abs(i - j)
    }
  }
  return(R)
}

n_time <- 11
rho_hat <- acf_mean$mean_acf[1]  # lag-1 ACF as initial estimate
cat("Estimated AR(1) rho:", round(rho_hat, 3), "\n")

R_ar1 <- make_ar1(n_time, rho = rho_hat)
```

### Toeplitz correlation matrix

The Toeplitz structure assigns a separate parameter for each lag:

$$
R_{ij} = \rho_{|t_i - t_j|}
$$

This is more flexible than AR(1) --- it does not enforce exponential decay.

```{r toeplitz-matrix}
make_toeplitz <- function(rho_vec) {
  n <- length(rho_vec) + 1
  R <- diag(n)
  for (lag in seq_along(rho_vec)) {
    for (i in seq_len(n - lag)) {
      R[i, i + lag] <- rho_vec[lag]
      R[i + lag, i] <- rho_vec[lag]
    }
  }
  # Ensure positive definiteness
  R <- as.matrix(Matrix::nearPD(R)$mat)
  return(R)
}

# Use the mean ACF values as lag-specific correlations
rho_toep <- acf_mean$mean_acf[1:min(10, nrow(acf_mean))]
R_toep <- make_toeplitz(rho_toep)
```

### MA(1) correlation matrix

The moving average (MA(1)) structure assumes that only adjacent time points
share correlation through a common shock:

$$
R_{ij} = \begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } |t_i - t_j| = 0 \\
  \theta / (1 + \theta^2) & \text{if } |t_i - t_j| = 1 \\
  0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

```{r ma1-matrix}
make_ma1 <- function(n_time, theta) {
  rho1 <- theta / (1 + theta^2)
  R <- diag(n_time)
  for (i in seq_len(n_time - 1)) {
    R[i, i + 1] <- rho1
    R[i + 1, i] <- rho1
  }
  return(R)
}

R_ma1 <- make_ma1(n_time, theta = 0.7)
```

### ARMA(1,1) correlation matrix

The ARMA(1,1) combines AR and MA components:

$$
R_{ij} = \begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } |t_i - t_j| = 0 \\
  \frac{(1 + \phi\theta)(\phi + \theta)}{1 + 2\phi\theta + \theta^2} \cdot \phi^{|t_i - t_j| - 1}
  & \text{if } |t_i - t_j| \geq 1
\end{cases}
$$

```{r arma11-matrix}
make_arma11 <- function(n_time, phi, theta) {
  rho1 <- (1 + phi * theta) * (phi + theta) / (1 + 2 * phi * theta + theta^2)
  R <- diag(n_time)
  for (i in seq_len(n_time)) {
    for (j in seq_len(n_time)) {
      lag <- abs(i - j)
      if (lag == 1) {
        R[i, j] <- rho1
      } else if (lag > 1) {
        R[i, j] <- rho1 * phi^(lag - 1)
      }
    }
  }
  R <- as.matrix(Matrix::nearPD(R)$mat)
  return(R)
}

R_arma <- make_arma11(n_time, phi = 0.8, theta = 0.3)
```

### Expanding to full data dimensions

The correlation matrices above are $T \times T$ (11 x 11). For `bayesreml`,
we need a block-diagonal matrix where each rat gets its own copy:

```{r block-expand}
make_block_diag <- function(R_base, group_factor) {
  groups <- levels(group_factor)
  n_total <- length(group_factor)
  R_full <- matrix(0, n_total, n_total)

  for (g in groups) {
    idx <- which(group_factor == g)
    n_g <- length(idx)
    # Handle cases where a rat may have fewer observations
    R_sub <- R_base[seq_len(n_g), seq_len(n_g)]
    R_full[idx, idx] <- R_sub
  }
  return(R_full)
}

# Create observation-level ID
bw$obs_id <- factor(seq_len(nrow(bw)))

# Ensure data is ordered by Rat and time_idx
bw <- bw[order(bw$Rat, bw$time_idx), ]
bw$obs_id <- factor(seq_len(nrow(bw)))

R_ar1_full  <- make_block_diag(R_ar1,  bw$Rat)
R_toep_full <- make_block_diag(R_toep, bw$Rat)
R_ma1_full  <- make_block_diag(R_ma1,  bw$Rat)
R_arma_full <- make_block_diag(R_arma, bw$Rat)
```

---

## 3. Model 14a: AR(1) temporal correlation

### Mathematical formulation

$$
y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_j + \beta \cdot t_k + (\alpha\beta)_{jk} + u_i
          + w_{ik} + \varepsilon_{ijk}
$$

where $u_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)$ is the random rat intercept and
$\mathbf{w}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_w^2 \mathbf{R}_{\text{AR1}})$
captures the temporal correlation.

### Fitting

```{r m14a-fit}
m_14a <- bayesreml(
  fixed          = weight ~ Diet * Time,
  random         = ~ Rat + vm(obs_id, Rar1),
  data           = bw,
  known_matrices = list(Rar1 = R_ar1_full),
  n_samples      = 2000,
  warmup         = 1000,
  chains         = 4
)
summary(m_14a)
```

### Diagnostics

```{r m14a-diag, fig.height = 6}
plot(m_14a, type = "diagnostics")
```

### ACF of corrected residuals

```{r m14a-acf, fig.height = 4}
bw$resid_14a <- residuals(m_14a)

acf_corrected <- bw %>%
  group_by(Rat) %>%
  summarise(
    acf_vals = list(acf(resid_14a, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 10)$acf[-1]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(acf_vals = lapply(acf_vals, function(x)
    data.frame(lag = seq_along(x), acf = as.numeric(x)))) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(acf_vals)

acf_corr_mean <- acf_corrected %>%
  group_by(lag) %>%
  summarise(mean_acf = mean(acf), .groups = "drop")

# Compare raw and corrected ACFs
acf_compare <- bind_rows(
  acf_mean %>% mutate(model = "Naive (no temporal)"),
  acf_corr_mean %>% mutate(model = "AR(1) corrected")
)

ggplot(acf_compare, aes(x = lag, y = mean_acf, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96) / sqrt(11),
             linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(title = "Mean ACF: naive vs AR(1)-corrected residuals",
       x = "Lag", y = "Autocorrelation", colour = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()
```

If the AR(1) model adequately captures the temporal correlation, the corrected
residuals should show no significant autocorrelation (all ACF values within the
dashed 95% bounds).

### AR(1) parameter interpretation

The AR(1) parameter $\rho$ controls the rate of correlation decay:

$$
\text{Cor}(y_t, y_{t+k}) = \rho^k
$$

```{r m14a-decay, fig.height = 4}
# Correlation decay plot
lags <- 0:10
decay_df <- data.frame(
  lag = lags,
  correlation = rho_hat^lags
)

ggplot(decay_df, aes(x = lag, y = correlation)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 2.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 0.5,
           label = paste0("rho = ", round(rho_hat, 3)),
           colour = "steelblue", size = 5) +
  labs(title = "AR(1) correlation decay",
       subtitle = "Correlation halves every log(2)/log(rho) lags",
       x = "Lag (time steps)", y = "Correlation") +
  theme_minimal()

half_life <- log(2) / (-log(abs(rho_hat)))
cat("Correlation half-life:", round(half_life, 2), "time steps\n")
```

### Spaghetti plot with fitted lines

```{r m14a-spaghetti, fig.height = 5}
bw$fitted_14a <- fitted(m_14a)

ggplot(bw, aes(x = Time, group = Rat)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = weight), alpha = 0.3, size = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_14a, colour = Diet), linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ Diet, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(title = "Model 14a: AR(1) fitted trajectories",
       x = "Time (days)", y = "Body weight (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## 4. Model 14b: Toeplitz structure

```{r m14b-fit}
m_14b <- bayesreml(
  fixed          = weight ~ Diet * Time,
  random         = ~ Rat + vm(obs_id, Rtoep),
  data           = bw,
  known_matrices = list(Rtoep = R_toep_full),
  n_samples      = 2000,
  warmup         = 1000,
  chains         = 4
)
summary(m_14b)
```

### Toeplitz lag-specific correlations

```{r m14b-lags, fig.height = 4}
# The Toeplitz structure uses separate rho for each lag
toep_df <- data.frame(
  lag = seq_along(rho_toep),
  correlation = rho_toep,
  ar1_comparison = rho_hat^seq_along(rho_toep)
)

toep_long <- toep_df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(correlation, ar1_comparison),
               names_to = "structure", values_to = "rho") %>%
  mutate(structure = recode(structure,
    correlation    = "Toeplitz (observed)",
    ar1_comparison = "AR(1) (fitted)"
  ))

ggplot(toep_long, aes(x = lag, y = rho, colour = structure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Toeplitz vs AR(1): lag-specific correlations",
       subtitle = "Deviations from the AR(1) line indicate non-exponential decay",
       x = "Lag", y = "Correlation", colour = "") +
  theme_minimal()
```

If the Toeplitz correlations closely follow the AR(1) curve, the simpler AR(1)
model is sufficient. Deviations suggest the true correlation structure is more
complex.

---

## 5. Model 14c: MA(1) structure

```{r m14c-fit}
m_14c <- bayesreml(
  fixed          = weight ~ Diet * Time,
  random         = ~ Rat + vm(obs_id, Rma1),
  data           = bw,
  known_matrices = list(Rma1 = R_ma1_full),
  n_samples      = 2000,
  warmup         = 1000,
  chains         = 4
)
summary(m_14c)
```

The MA(1) model implies that the correlation drops to zero after lag 1. This is
rarely appropriate for growth data where correlation persists across many lags.

---

## 6. Model 14d: ARMA(1,1) structure

```{r m14d-fit}
m_14d <- bayesreml(
  fixed          = weight ~ Diet * Time,
  random         = ~ Rat + vm(obs_id, Rarma),
  data           = bw,
  known_matrices = list(Rarma = R_arma_full),
  n_samples      = 2000,
  warmup         = 1000,
  chains         = 4
)
summary(m_14d)
```

## 7. Structure comparison

### Model comparison via DIC

```{r compare-dic}
anova(m_14a, m_14b, m_14c, m_14d)
```

### ACF comparison across models

```{r compare-acf, fig.height = 6}
bw$resid_14b <- residuals(m_14b)
bw$resid_14c <- residuals(m_14c)
bw$resid_14d <- residuals(m_14d)

compute_mean_acf <- function(data, resid_col, model_name) {
  data %>%
    group_by(Rat) %>%
    summarise(
      acf_vals = list(acf(.data[[resid_col]], plot = FALSE,
                          lag.max = 10)$acf[-1]),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(acf_vals = lapply(acf_vals, function(x)
      data.frame(lag = seq_along(x), acf = as.numeric(x)))) %>%
    tidyr::unnest(acf_vals) %>%
    group_by(lag) %>%
    summarise(mean_acf = mean(acf), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(model = model_name)
}

acf_all <- bind_rows(
  acf_mean %>% mutate(model = "Naive"),
  compute_mean_acf(bw, "resid_14a", "AR(1)"),
  compute_mean_acf(bw, "resid_14b", "Toeplitz"),
  compute_mean_acf(bw, "resid_14c", "MA(1)"),
  compute_mean_acf(bw, "resid_14d", "ARMA(1,1)")
)

ggplot(acf_all, aes(x = lag, y = mean_acf, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96) / sqrt(11),
             linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(title = "Residual ACF comparison across temporal structures",
       x = "Lag", y = "Mean autocorrelation", colour = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Time-series prediction with credible bands

```{r predict-bands, fig.height = 5}
# Population-level prediction for Diet 1
new_time <- data.frame(
  Diet = factor(1, levels = levels(bw$Diet)),
  Time = seq(min(bw$Time), max(bw$Time) * 1.2, length.out = 50)
)

pred_14a <- predict(m_14a, newdata = new_time, se.fit = TRUE)
new_time$fit   <- pred_14a$fit
new_time$lower <- pred_14a$fit - 1.96 * pred_14a$se.fit
new_time$upper <- pred_14a$fit + 1.96 * pred_14a$se.fit

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = new_time, aes(x = Time, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = new_time, aes(x = Time, y = fit),
            colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = bw[bw$Diet == 1, ], aes(x = Time, y = weight),
             alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = max(bw$Time), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "red", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = max(bw$Time) * 1.05, y = max(bw$weight) * 0.9,
           label = "extrapolation", colour = "red", size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "AR(1) model: prediction with 95% credible band",
       subtitle = "Diet 1, population-level (random effects integrated out)",
       x = "Time (days)", y = "Body weight (g)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Comparison with nlme

```{r compare-nlme}
lme_ar1 <- lme(weight ~ Diet * Time, random = ~ 1 | Rat,
               correlation = corAR1(form = ~ time_idx | Rat),
               data = bw)
summary(lme_ar1)

# Compare fixed effects
data.frame(
  Parameter = names(coef(m_14a)),
  bayesreml = round(coef(m_14a), 3),
  nlme      = round(fixef(lme_ar1), 3)
)

# Compare AR(1) parameter
intervals(lme_ar1, which = "var-cov")$corStruct
cat("bayesreml AR(1) rho (input):", round(rho_hat, 3), "\n")
```

## 8. ACF diagnostic chart

A comprehensive ACF diagnostic panel:

```{r acf-panel, fig.height = 7}
# Per-rat ACF for the best model
best_resid <- "resid_14a"  # change based on model comparison results

acf_per_rat <- bw %>%
  group_by(Rat, Diet) %>%
  summarise(
    acf_vals = list(acf(.data[[best_resid]], plot = FALSE,
                        lag.max = 8)$acf[-1]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(acf_vals = lapply(acf_vals, function(x)
    data.frame(lag = seq_along(x), acf = as.numeric(x)))) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(acf_vals)

ggplot(acf_per_rat, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96) / sqrt(11),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ Rat, ncol = 4) +
  labs(title = "Per-rat ACF of AR(1)-corrected residuals",
       subtitle = "Bars outside dashed lines indicate residual autocorrelation",
       x = "Lag", y = "ACF") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8))
```

---

## 9. Key takeaways

1. **Inspect the ACF before and after fitting.** The raw residual ACF motivates
   the choice of temporal structure. The corrected residual ACF validates that
   the chosen structure is adequate.

2. **AR(1) is the default starting point** for longitudinal data with regularly
   spaced time points. Its single parameter ($\rho$) is interpretable as the
   correlation between adjacent measurements.

3. **Toeplitz is a diagnostic tool.** If the Toeplitz lag-specific correlations
   closely follow the AR(1) exponential decay, the simpler model suffices.

4. **MA(1) is rarely sufficient** for growth data because it implies zero
   correlation beyond lag 1. It is more appropriate for processes driven by
   transient shocks.

5. **ARMA(1,1) combines both mechanisms** and can capture correlation patterns
   that neither AR(1) nor MA(1) alone can model. The extra parameter must be
   justified by model comparison.

6. **Temporal correlation matrices must be block-diagonal** when subjects are
   independent. Each subject gets its own $T \times T$ block within the
   $N \times N$ full matrix.

7. **Extrapolation** beyond the observed time range is risky. The credible
   bands widen dramatically, reflecting increasing uncertainty.

```{r show-code}
cat(m_14a$extras$code)
```
